items.prompt: In a group discussion, what should you do when someone else is talking?

options.text: Listen and wait for your turn.

options.why: Then nobody can be heard.

options.text: Look away and play with something.
options.why: This shows you are not listening.
You cannot take part if you leave.

hints: Think about how you want others to act when you talk.
A discussion needs everyone to be heard.
Which answer helps the speaker most?
items.explanation: Good discussions take turns. Listening carefully also helps you reply to what others say.

items.prompt: Which is a polite way to disagree?

options.why: This is unkind, and it gives no reason.
This is rude, and it does not explain why.

options.text: I see what you mean, but I think a fish would be easier to look after.

options.why: This stops the discussion.

hints: Polite disagreement respects the other person.
It shows you listened before you give your view.
Look for a sentence that also gives a reason.
items.explanation: I see what you mean shows you listened. Then but I think gives your own view, with a reason, politely.

items.prompt: Which sentence gives an opinion and a reason?

options.text: I think we should plant trees.
options.why: This gives an opinion, but no reason.
One word is not an opinion with a reason.
This asks for someone else's opinion.

options.text: I think we should plant trees because they give us shade.

hints: An opinion says what you think.
A reason explains why.
Look for the word that introduces a reason.
items.explanation: I think shows the opinion, and because they give us shade is the reason.

items.prompt: Your group must choose a class pet. How can you make sure everyone has a say?

options.why: Quieter people would not be heard.

options.text: Ask each person for their idea in turn.

options.why: Then nobody else gets a say.

options.text: Only listen to your best friend.
options.why: Everyone in the group should be heard.

hints: Think about the quieter people in the group.
How can each person get a turn?
Which answer includes everyone?
items.explanation: Asking each person in turn means that the quieter people are heard too.

items.prompt: Which is the best way to sum up a discussion?

options.why: This does not say what the group decided, or why.

options.text: I want a dog and that's it.
options.why: This is one person's wish, not a summary.

options.text: So, most of us think a fish would be the best class pet, because it is easy to look after.

options.why: This does not say what was decided.

hints: A summary tells what the group decided.
It also gives the main reason.
Which answer would help someone who missed the discussion?
items.explanation: A good summary says what most people agreed and why. It helps everyone remember the decision.

items.prompt: Give your opinion. Should children have homework every day? Give at least two reasons.

criteria.label: I gave a clear opinion
I gave at least two reasons
I used linking words like because, also and however
I spoke clearly and at a good speed

hints: Start with: I think... because...
Use Also for your second reason.
items.explanation: A strong spoken opinion is clear, gives reasons and links them with words like because and also.

items.prompt: Your friend says, “Rainy days are boring.” Do you agree? Explain why or why not, politely.

criteria.label: I said politely whether I agree or disagree
I gave reasons or examples
I used a polite phrase like I see what you mean, but...

hints: Start by showing that you heard your friend.
Give an example of something you do on rainy days.
items.explanation: Polite disagreement shows respect: it mentions the other view kindly, then gives reasons for your own.

items.prompt: Give a one-minute talk about an animal that lives in Indonesia. Use facts you know.

criteria.label: I introduced my animal clearly
I gave several true facts
I organised my talk, such as where it lives, then what it eats
I looked up and spoke clearly

hints: Plan your talk like a report with sections.
End with your most interesting fact.
items.explanation: A good short talk is organised like a report, with a clear start, facts in a sensible order and a strong ending.

items.prompt: Read this part of a persuasive letter aloud. Imagine you are speaking to the whole school.
items.readText: A refill station would help in several ways. Firstly, there would be less plastic rubbish. Plastic bottles can take hundreds of years to break down, and some of them end up in rivers and the sea. Secondly, families would save money, because pupils could bring the same bottle every day.

criteria.label: I read every word correctly
I used a strong, confident voice
I paused after each reason
I stressed important words like Firstly and Secondly

hints: Practise once quietly first.
Pause at each full stop.
items.explanation: Persuasive speaking uses a confident voice, clear pauses and stress on the key words.

items.prompt: Your class is choosing a trip: the zoo or the science museum. Say which you would choose and why. Then answer one reason someone might give for the other place.

criteria.label: I made my choice clear
I gave at least two reasons
I answered a reason for the other place, politely
I finished with a short summary
I spoke clearly and confidently

hints: Use: Some people might say... However...
Finish with: So, I think we should...
items.explanation: Answering the other side shows that you have listened and thought about it, which makes your argument stronger.

items.prompt: Think about this idea: every school should have a vegetable garden. Give one reason for it and one reason against it. Then say what you think.

criteria.label: I gave a reason for the idea
I gave a reason against the idea
I gave my own opinion with a reason
I used phrases like on the other hand

hints: Start with: One reason for this is...
Then say: On the other hand...
items.explanation: Looking at both sides before giving your own opinion is what good discussions do.

items.prompt: Which sentence is a polite way to disagree?

options.why: This is rude and does not listen to the person.
This could upset your friend.

options.text: I am not listening to you.
options.why: A discussion needs listening.

options.text: I see your point, but I think we should try a different way.

hints: Polite words respect the other person.
Start by showing you listened.
Which choice uses but to give your own idea?
items.explanation: A polite reply shows you heard the idea and then gives your own view.

items.prompt: Put the steps of taking part in a group discussion in order.
items: Listen to the topic or question.
Think about what you want to say.
Wait for a gap, then speak.
Give your idea and a reason.
hints: You cannot answer before you listen.
Thinking comes before speaking.
Listening to replies comes last.
items.explanation: Listen first, think, wait for your turn, speak with a reason, then listen again.

items.prompt: Sort each action into helpful or unhelpful in a discussion.
hints: Good discussion habits show respect.
Which actions make others feel ignored?
Start with looking at the speaker.
items.explanation: Looking, building on ideas and asking questions help everyone. Interrupting and eye-rolling show disrespect.

items.prompt: Leo says, "I think we should have a bake sale." Which reply builds on his idea?

options.why: This stops the discussion without a reason.

options.text: I want to talk about something else.
options.why: This ignores Leo's idea.

options.text: Good idea, and we could also sell lemonade.

options.why: This is unkind and gives no reason.

hints: Building on an idea means adding to it.
Which reply uses the word also?
A good reply shows you listened.
items.explanation: Adding lemonade shows the speaker listened and made the idea bigger.

items.prompt: Choose all the phrases that help you give a reason for your idea.

options.why: Whatever does not give a reason.
These are filler words.

hints: A reason answers the question why.
Which words link an idea to its cause?
Two choices are only filler.
items.explanation: Because, since and that is why link an idea to a reason. Whatever and um, like do not.

items.prompt: Two children want different games, and the group cannot agree. What is the best way to decide?

options.why: This is not fair to everyone.
The problem would not be solved.
The group should decide fairly together.

options.text: Listen to each reason, then vote or find a plan that suits both.

hints: Fair groups listen before they decide.
Think about voting or finding a middle way.
Cross out the choices that are unfair.
items.explanation: A fair group hears every reason and then votes or finds a compromise.

items.prompt: At the end of a discussion, the teacher asks you to sum up. What should you do?

options.why: A summary must be short.

options.text: Say the main points the group agreed on, in a few words.

options.why: Summing up covers what was already said.
A summary is not about blaming anyone.

hints: To sum up means to make something short.
Focus on what the group agreed.
Keep it brief.
items.explanation: A good summary gives the main points of the discussion, briefly and fairly.
